title: Face-Off With China Continues at Multiple Points on Arunachal Border, ITBP Chief Says
excerpt: Director General Praveen Kumar says the eastern-sector standoff persists even as peace efforts continue — and that the ITBP has raised drone units across all commands along the LAC.
body:
• ITBP Director General Praveen Kumar says the face-off with China continues at multiple locations along the Arunachal Pradesh border, even as both sides manage the Line of Actual Control.
  • The force has raised specialised drone units in all its commands and deployed them along the LAC as part of a modernisation drive that accelerated after the 2020 Galwan clash.
  • The ITBP guards the 3,488-km India-China border; Kumar's remarks came at the force's Raising Day events this week.
  • For readers tracking the relationship: the comments are a status report, not an escalation alert — no new clash was reported, but disengagement has plainly not ended the standoff in the eastern sector.

The standoff with China in the eastern Himalayas is not over. Indo-Tibetan Border Police Director General Praveen Kumar said this week that "the face-off with China continues at multiple locations along Arunachal border," even as the two countries work to maintain peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC). The remarks, carried by The Hindu, are the clearest recent confirmation from the force that guards the border that friction in the Arunachal sector persists years after the 2020 crisis began.

Drones Join the Mountain Force

Kumar used the ITBP's Raising Day events to outline a force being rebuilt for a different kind of border watch. According to PTI reporting via Rediff, the ITBP has raised specialised drone units in all its commands and deployed them along the LAC, alongside a broader modernisation of surveillance and communications. The force is also training and equipping its personnel for the kind of close confrontation seen at Galwan in 2020, when a hand-to-hand clash in Ladakh killed 20 Indian soldiers and reset the border's rules of engagement.

https://x.com/Jairam_Ramesh/status/2113465845565575268

The ITBP is the first line on the 3,488-km India-China frontier, manning high-altitude posts through Himalayan winters. Its modernisation sits inside a wider Indian build-up along the LAC — new roads, tunnels, airfields and habitat for troops — meant to close an infrastructure gap with China that the 2020 standoff exposed.

Peace at the Table, Posture on the Ground

Kumar's framing was deliberate: efforts to maintain peace continue, and the face-off continues. That duality has defined the relationship since the 2020 Galwan clash — disengagement agreements at specific friction points, corps-commander talks, and a partial normalisation of diplomacy, alongside tens of thousands of troops and new hardware held in position on both sides. The eastern sector, where China claims Arunachal Pradesh as its own, has seen its own flashpoints, including the December 2022 clash at Yangtse near Tawang.

For the diaspora following India's security from abroad, the takeaway is calibration. No new incident accompanied the ITBP chief's remarks; this was a readiness report from a force modernising for a long watch — drones overhead, better kit on the ground, and a border that, in his words, remains a face-off at multiple locations. The next signals to watch are the corps-commander talks and any announced change in force posture on either side; until then, the mountain standoff is a managed condition, not a resolved one.
